speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had a very useful discussion yesterday with the Minister of Industry and Commerce for the province of Quebec. We reviewed the state of the industry, as I have done with others including Liberal members of parliament who have made many representations to me in respect of the condition of the industry, and I have had discussions with the industry itself. subtopic: AGRICULTURE
subsubtopic: CHANGES IN SUBSIDY FORMULA FOR INDUSTRIAL MILK AND CREAM PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would have much preferred it if some other minister had made his statement on this first occasion. I understood my statement was to be brief. I will try to be brief.
For some time the members of the dairy industry and the government have been working to build a long-term dairy policy. Working together, we formed the Canadian Dairy Commission in 1967. That was a big step in the right direction. It saved dairy farmers from abrupt swings in the market. It also provided security against barrel-bottom prices to milk producers. Now it is time to take the next step. That is why, starting today, the returns to industrial milk and cream producers will be adjusted to changing production costs. We will use a formula to do this.
As you know, at the beginning of each April a new dairy year begins and producers wait anxiously to hear the government announce the support levels for the coming year. Rapid increases in the prices of dairy inputs have made their situation even more urgent. Dairy farmers have to tie up too much money in land, buildings, and stock to live from year to year. That is the reason behind our move to formula pricing. It will give needed security to both producers and consumers.
This formula will gear industrial milk and cream producers' incomes to input prices. What it means to the efficient, hard-working farmer is that neither inflation nor a big jump in cash costs will leave him in an income squeeze. To consumers this will mean a constant supply of nutrition-packed milk. Although it will guarantee producers a fair return, consumers should realize that this also will protect them from rip-off milk prices at the farm gate.

Future changes in support levels will reflect changes in labour and cash costs which will make up 80 per cent of the formula. Forty-five per cent of this formula is based on the cash costs of producing milk. Thirty-five per cent is based on labour earnings adjusted by the consumer price index. In addition, a number of other supply and demand factors will be taken into account.
If, midway in the dairy year, the returns adjustment formula goes up or down more than 4 per cent, this will result in a change in producer returns. This change, up or down, will come from the marketplace. The support levels will not be changed more often than once every three months. It is important to understand that the government will be reducing direct support payments to dairy producers. Our aim, over the long haul, is to have producers get every cent of their income from the marketplace.

The important paragraph of the minister's statement is as follows: "It is important to understand that the government will be reducing direct support payments to dairy producers. Our aim, over the long haul, is to have producers get every cent of their income from the marketplace."
The minister said in his statement, and I quote: "When people call milk the perfect food, they are right on target." The minister has a great capacity for stating the obvious as though it were a revelation from the supernatural. If milk were the perfect food and if it is essential, particularly for children, then almost every country in the world should have subsidized milk production, both to the producers and the consumers. The United States has a school lunch program and free milk. For years the United Kingdom has had subsidized basic foods, of which milk is one. pay-
What is the minister now announcing? Having cancelled the consumer subsidy a few months ago, the minister is now telling us they are going to reduce the direct support payments. Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to deplore very briefly the offhand and jesting manner in which the minister announced a policy which will have such serious effects.

Mr. Speaker, the minister announced today that, from now on, dairy policy will be based on input costs, including 45 per cent production costs and 35 per cent manpower costs. The minister said that, from now on, this policy will be reviewed every three months instead of once a year, on April 1. Mr. Speaker, I do not have confidence in the statement of the minister for a very simple reason. Last year, the minister announced a consumer subsidy. Indeed, the government invested $109 million for this purpose, but at the same time it imported 24,749,000 pounds of milk at an average rate of 54 cents a pound, which it sold at an average price of 95 cents. In other words, the government took from the consumer what it had politically announced as being a consumer subsidy. In fact, the consumer had to pay. subtopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACTS, 1867 TO 1965 AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION FOR YUKON AND NORTHWEST TERRITORIES

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council) moved
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACTS, 1867 TO 1965 AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION FOR YUKON AND NORTHWEST TERRITORIES
speechtext:
that Bill C-3, to amend the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1965, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to amend the British North America Acts to provide for the appointment of one senator from each of the Northwest and Yukon Territories.
Hon. members are aware of the concern of the government that all regions of Canada should receive fair representation in both Houses of parliament. This aim has been achieved with regard to this Chamber with the enactment of the Representation Act, 1974, and the Northwest Territories Representation Act. Equitable representation in the House of Commons is by no means sufficient, however; we must achieve equitable representation in parliament as a whole. It is essential that the northern viewpoint should find expression in the other place, just as do the views of all other parts of Canada.
This is not a partisan matter, Mr. Speaker. Nor is this the first time the matter has been before parliament. In the second session of the 29th parliament the House gave second reading to Bill C-ll, which was identical in terms to the bill now before us, Bill C-3. At that time my predecessor in office pointed out that in the early days of confederation before the creation of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, the Territories were represented in the Senate as well as in the Commons.
Moreoever, the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) has introduced a private member's bill to the same effect as Bill C-3. As hon. members are aware, the government was willing to support the passage of that member's bill until it became evident that there were technical problems which could not be resolved.
It is of fundamental importance to this country that the north should be justly represented in parliament, and I am sure this will be recognized by all hon. members in their consideration of this measure.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks on this matter will be very brief. I think the
April 18, 1975

time taken up with the introduction of this bill in the House is a waste.
When we get the Liberals and the Conservatives together on a measure to provide for the residents of the Northwest and Yukon Territories, a measure they consider to be some kind of a plum, it arouses some suspicion in my mind. Had the two parties got together and suggested the appointment of an ombudsman, or someone of that nature, who could do something for the people of the Northwest and Yukon Territories, I can assure the House they would have received a great deal of support. I see no merit whatever in this idea on which the Liberals and the Conservatives are in agreement. This is a waste of money, and the people of the north have not asked for and do not want anything like this. I do not think any self-respecting northerner would accept such a measure.
Should this bill be approved by this House, and that seems very likely since the Liberals and Conservatives are together on it, it will discriminate to a large extent against the native population of these territories. If hon. members will look at Section 23(4) of the British North America Act they will find that, among the qualifications required to become a senator, a candidate must personally have real property over and above his debts to a value of $4,000. I should like anyone to travel throughout the Northwest and Yukon Territories and point out to me a number of native people who are in that position. I am sure they will find the number to be very small. Just yesterday-

Do you want to be one of the representatives of the north?
Just yesterday before the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development some figures were read out to us by the representatives from the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. They referred to the income of the people in the Northwest Territories. That is on the record and shows that the income level for the majority of the northern native people is under $1,000. The accepted poverty level for the country, I believe, is somewhere in the neighbourhood of $3,500. I suggest this discriminates to a large extent against the northern native people.
I should like to reiterate the point that I would rather see this thing scrapped and sent to the junk yard. We would prefer having an ombudsman representing both territories. This could be accomplished with one third the cost of having a senator from each territory who would not be representative. In addition this would amount to the appointment of either a Liberal or Conservative hack, who perhaps would be a campaign manager in forthcoming election campaigns. At the present time I think the Liberals are indicating some kind of desperation over the fact that they do not have representation from either territory, and therefore they intend to take some more of the taxpayer's money which will be wasted in an effort to obtain some representation from that part of the country. I made a slip-that would not be representation at all, Mr. Speaker.
Senate Representation
I hope that this bill does not pass but, if it should pass and should be referred to the committee, I hope that we will have in attendance there representatives from the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory, and from their councils, because I am sure they will say what the people from that part of the country believe about this matter. I am almost certain they will echo the sentiments I have expressed at this time. I shall waste no more time on this matter.

subtopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACTS, 1867 TO 1965 AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SENATE REPRESENTATION FOR YUKON AND NORTHWEST TERRITORIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I always respect the remarks and the feelings expressed by the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth), I should say I am a little disappointed this morning to hear him accuse the Liberals and Conservatives of getting together in a sort of conspiracy to deal with this bill. Hon. members should be aware that we in this party have never gone to bed with the government. I look back on the twenty-ninth parliament and recall vividly the actions of the party to my left in dealing with the government of that day. I can assure the hon. member that there is no conspiracy at this time on our part to co-operate with the government. We do feel, however, that this bill is necessary and should be passed.
I have no intention of making a lengthy speech on the subject this morning, but I do recall that a week or ten days ago we were dealing with amendments to the Northern Canada Power Corporation Bill. While that bill was in committee we heard from various groups and representatives of the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories. They made representations and suggestions concerning how that particular bill should be dealt with, and nearly without exception the members of those various groups and organizations indicated they were looking forward to the day when both the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories would attain provincial status. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan) and the staff of that department taking part in the committee hearings indicated it was their feeling that we should work toward the day when both these territories would attain provincial status.
I feel this particular bill is one more step toward giving both territories provincial status. It moves us one step closer toward attaining that status, which I believe is what the people of the territories and all members of this House want. Over the years there has been much criticism of the other place. Much of that criticism has been deserved. Over the years appointments to the other place has become a means of paying the political debts of the party in power to those people on the hustings who worked on its behalf.
That was not the intention of the Fathers of Confederation when they set up our constitution and provided for the Senate. They felt there was a need and a place for a Senate in the government of our country, and that the Senate would serve a useful function. The Senate should be made up of a balance of representatives from the various political parties. This is not the situation at the present time.
Before I came down to the House I looked at the parliamentary guide, and noted that recent figures show that the representation in the Senate is made up of 85 per cent of appointees by the government and some 15 per cent of

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I called it one o'clock I was referring to the imbalance in representation in the Senate and I mentioned that at present about 85 per cent of the Senators are Liberal appointees, about 15 per cent are Conservative appointees, and there is a small handful of independents. I think it is important to point it out, because this imbalance creates such a situation that I do not believe the Senate can function properly.
It seems to me that the government should quickly call together a committee made up of representatives of all parties in the House to study and examine the Senate as it stands at present, to give consideration to the reorganization of the other place, and to see what changes we can make in the Senate to enable it to make a sound and active contribution to the government of the country.
In the meantime I hope that the government will give serious consideration to the manner and method of appointment of the two Senators for the territories. I hope that the amendments that we have before us today in Bill C-3 were made for the purpose of making positions available for people of integrity, people who could contribute, and not just for the purpose of making a place for some political hack. I feel it is important in both cases that the person who is appointed should have stature in the territory and the respect of the residents of that territory. He or she should be a person who has been a leader in the area, should be a person who is apolitical, and does not have political ties.
Furthermore, I think serious consideration should be given to naming a native person as a Senator from one of the territories, preferably someone of the Inuit race. The hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) has

indicated that he feels that under the present provisions in the BNA Act it would be almost impossible for any native person in the territories to qualify as a Senator. I have had the opportunity to examine the BNA act and I find that under 23(3) there is a requirement that anyone who is appointed to the Senate own lands to the value of $4,000 over and above his debts and liabilities. I realize that many of the native people in the territories could not qualify because they do not own land in their own right.
I feel it is incumbent on the government to bring in an amendment to the BNA Act with respect to native people to permit them to qualify as Senators without having to comply with these specific requirements. I believe that if the government, in filling these key positions, follows the criteria that I have mentioned, it will show the public that the Senate does have a place in the government of our country and it can serve a useful function.
On the other hand, if the government proceeds in the same manner as it has in the past with regard to the appointment of Senators, I am sure that the public will continue to feel that the Senate is a rather useless place to which we send people who have served their political parties over the years. We on this side, as well as the public generally, are looking forward with interest to seeing who the candidates will be for appointments in the Senate from the Northwest Territories and the Yukon.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak for only a moment on this subject. I thought that since there has been so much concentration from the other side on who might be appointed to these positions, we should rather think for a moment about the principle underlying this legislation.
I am very pleased that three years after the special joint committee on the constitution of Canada presented its report to the House and the other place, the government is now bringing forward in legislative form many of the recommendations of that committee.
I think the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth), who just spoke, had a point when he mentioned the difficulties to be faced in the appointment of a person of native race to the Senate. This relates not so much to the bill before us, however, as to the requirements for a member of the Senate. If he and other hon. members look at the report of the special joint committee they will find that we had something to say on this point as well. It is high time that the present qualifications were changed, not by way of exceptions for the native people, although indeed they are worthy of exception if one were needed, but because such qualifications are now purely anachronistic.
We do not need another study or commission to consider what needs to be done with the Senate. That question was canvassed by the joint committee on the constitution, and those of us who served felt that, as at the time of confederation itself, this was the single most controversial question before the committee. After some meetings we were able to come up with a consensus on the Senate which included doubling the number of senators from western

This bill is something which is overdue. I am very pleased that it is now before us, and I hope it will be followed by other pieces of legislation also emanating from the report of the committee on the constitution.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this bill. I certainly agree with the purpose of the bill which is to give the Northwest Territories and the Yukon representation in Canada's second chamber. I think that, more than most, this bill will provide a means of fulfilling representation at a level of government which is represented by area. I shall speak on this a little later in relation to our problems on redistribution in this chamber and the relationship of the other place to this chamber in representing areas in Canada.
I believe that the Senate has a recognized role in our government. Even though it is balanced in favour of one political party I feel it does give some input to our governmental process.
I feel that more could be done by the Senate, perhaps by way of introducing bills that are not controversial but are highly technical, because I think the Senate has more time for such study. They have people who can give considerable thought to bills of a special nature such as commercial, financial or cultural, and perhaps they are not quite so restricted by party politics as we in this chamber. Unfortunately, at the present time there are not enough people to give the Conservative viewpoint, but nevertheless I feel that the other place has contributed to the work of this chamber.
On occasion I have been critical of Senate committees although I can think of such worth-while endeavours as the Senate Committee on Poverty and the good job a committee did on the white paper on taxation. I believe that work was useful to us in considering the subsequent legislation.
When considering the recent redistribution of seats, the problem of representation at Ottawa came to the fore. We in the House of Commons have endeavoured to have representation by population. By allowing up to 25 per cent tolerance between urban and rural ridings we recognize that such small provinces as Prince Edward Island have less representation than they are entitled to were they strictly represented by population. Similarly, New Brunswick has less members than is normal. There has been considerable discussion about whether some of these voids might be filled by a better balance in the Senate, and whether the other place could fulfil something that the House of Commons does not.
Whether we like it or not we have always had a great deal of regional government. One region of the country has been dominant in government for some time, and then has been replaced by a predominance from another region. There is no doubt that the province of Quebec and central Canada, with their large populations, have made the rest of the country seem like onlookers on the government scene. This imbalance might be removed to some extent by having representation in the other place that would protect the smaller provinces.
Senate Representation
It is perhaps significant that provinces like Ontario and Quebec are in the centre of the country, flanked by the relatively small four eastern provinces and the four western provinces which are not small but have nothing like the population of Quebec and Ontario. If the western provinces and the maritimes had the population, and Ontario and Quebec were divided into smaller provinces, of course it would have been a different country.
I think we could look at the possibility of the provinces having a hand in making appointments to the other place when vacancies occur. As the west matures I think there is a growing feeling there that it is not adequately represented in Ottawa, and if this feeling persists it could lead to even greater regional strains than we already have.
The tradition of appointments to the other place being made by the party in power may have seemed a good thing in the beginning, and had the political parties alternated with reasonable frequency perhaps no great harm would have been done. I think there is much to be said for keeping close to this House those people who have finished serving their time as members. Let us keep them near us so that they can offer us the benefit of their political experience. Their opinions will be valuable in giving cohesion to our political process.

The Conservative party was the governing party in the first years after confederation, but the Liberal party has governed for most of the past 60 years. Consequently representation in the other place is not balanced. That is why I think an alternative way of making appointments should be considered.
Canada is a regional country. When the pendulum swings back and allows the Conservatives to assume power, it is possible my party will stay in power for as long as the Liberals have governed. This would be in accordance with the nature of our country. It is a regional country and we must do our best to give cohesiveness to this regionalism. I suggest that we have not fully taken this into account in our appointments to the other place. Perhaps it may be desirable to establish a committee of this House, to consider how there might be a better balance in future in the appointment of members to the other place.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to support the bill of my colleague, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp).
Dealing with the comment raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), the concept of the bill is not new. Prior to 1905 the Northwest Territories were represented by four members of the Senate, when the Territories included all of what is now the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, a large part of Manitoba, the northern part of Ontario and the northern part of Quebec. With the creation of the two new provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, these Senate seats were allocated to them. Since then suggestions have been made from time to time, and from various quarters, to correct this situation and provide the north with a larger voice in parliament.
Members recently indicated their support for this principle when they gave approval to Bill C-51, to create a second seat in this chamber for the Northwest Territories. Today we have an opportunity to go one step further, and I sincerely hope that all members will lend their support to this measure.
The people of the north are developing an increasing interest and awareness of their affairs. They wish to participate more actively at all levels. I am sure that both the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) and the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) will attest to this.
I might add that the Northwest Territories Council is on record as supporting the provision of territorial representation in the Senate. The Council's representatives made this point clear when they appeared before the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development approximately one year ago and indicated that the Council had unanimously endorsed this bill when it was before the previous parliament. I have no doubt the people of the Northwest Territories look forward to being represented in both Houses of Parliament again. Nor do I have any doubt that the people of the Yukon want their own Senator.
[Mr. Lambert (Edmonton West).)
It is as important to increase the northern voice at the national level as it is at the territorial and municipal levels. The provision of Senate seats for the two territories will provide additional opportunities for the expression of the northern viewpoint in parliament, and improve communications between Ottawa and the two territories at the parliamentary level. I have no hesitation in recommending that all hon. members give favourable consideration to this bill.

himself-particularly so on this point.
In so far as hon. members make strictures with regard to the other place, I would like to say that they are perhaps lucky that in the other place they do not make strictures about reducing the size of this overgrown chamber, and I may say I can say that because I am a member of this place. The proposal to bloat it out of proportion that we blithely adopted in the legislation considered earlier this session was a serious mistake, I think, for the future operation of this chamber. Be that as it may, I would hope that some hon. members feel that some of the more able of their colleagues or contemporaries in the other place would be restrained or constrained from making similar remarks about eliminating parts of the House of Commons, or perhaps one of these days we will see a proposal in the other place to do precisely what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre tries to do at a stroke of the pen, likely his own, to wipe out the other part. That is the easiest way to eliminate differences of opinion-just strike them out.
I can think of no greater danger in Canadian democracy than the tyranny of a temporary majority. We have seen temporary majorities here run away with ideas. In 1970, for instance-and I know the hon. member will gladly subscribe to this-in October, 1970 it was a temporary runaway majority, a stampede of opinion, which created terrible precedents in this country, and we will live to regret it.
I welcome the provision now before us if only, Mr. Speaker, because many times in schools that I visit in my constituency I am asked to trace through the structure of Canadian government in Canada. I am asked to trace back
April 18, 1975

to the days of Confederation and to say why the Senate was proposed, why it was established.
Some people feel the world was discovered yesterday. But many of the problems faced in Canada today are merely a translation into a present-day picture of a problem which existed in the 18th century, for example, the question of disparity of language, the disparity of people in the Atlantic provinces as compared with those of Central Canada.
It is heard quite frequently, both in the Atlantic provinces as well as out in the west, that the people in Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal think that all that is good for Canada are the things that are good for their areas. In other words, if it's good for Central Canada it has to be good for the rest of Canada. It is precisely that spirit which existed in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island back in the 1860's. One of the ways to counteract this oppression by population, this potential injustice, was to have a Senate in which the representation was disproportionate. In other words, by giving 24 Senate seats to the Atlantic provinces, 24 to Lower Canada, 24 to Upper Canada and 24, in the end, to Western Canada, some counterbalance was created against this mass of population in favour of smaller regions with smaller populations. That was the theory. It hasn't always worked out.
I think that the constitution of the Senate, that is, the naming of members, the practices of governments and prime ministers, all have eroded the proper status of Senate representation. I think the Senate has far greater potential than has been expressed by it. After all, it lies within the hands of government first of all to appoint members, and I think the government could quite readily name individuals to the Senate from all parts of the country, whether or not they are necessarily recognized by reason of party service, or have been effective political bagmen, or wanted to become effective bagmen, or because they are needed on some kind of part-time salary ready to become national chairmen, or for any other ulterior reason.
But even among those men who are appointed for the reasons I have outlined, I must say that there have been some excellent workers in so far as the country is concerned. There have been men and women of energy, and I do not wish to pick out any particular individuals. However, let me say that I do not think that outside commentators should point at one or two individuals in the Senate and condemn the whole institution. If it were all right to do such things, then some of the reputations in this House would not be very high either. Of course, the same could be said of newspaper editors, university professors, by anybody who wished to cast stones. They need only pick the poorest representatives in their class and give them a general classification, and we would all be in the same boat, somewhere down at the bottom of the heap.
Notwithstanding what the hon. member for Northwest Territories had to say this morning, I do not see that an ombudsman named both for the Yukon and the Northwest Territories would add one cubit to the effectiveness of government for the people in that area. Is it to be an

ombudsman between the people and the Northwest Territories council, the administration there, or between Yukoners and the Yukon administration, or is it to be an ombudsman vis-a-vis the whole of the federal administration?
So far we have not appointed a federal ombudsman, and I may say that I am not too sure it would be as effective as a provincial ombudsman. I do not know that a federal ombudsman is necessarily the answer but, leaving that aside, so far as representation of the people in the territories is concerned, it seems to me that we have a classic example of a territory that so far is economically lightly developed, with a very small population, in the same way as we would consider, say, Prince Edward Island was at the time of confederation.

Mr. Speaker, he tells me I have to be careful. I am not talking about their intellectual development. If my leader continues this too far he might find himself in trouble in Yellowknife! Let us look at the relative picture. I think there is some similarity between the time of confederation and today in terms of the degree of population, the density of population, of Prince Edward Island and Upper Canada, compared with the territories vis-a-vis what we call southern Canada, and so far as the relative degree of economic development is concerned.
Looking back 115 years, in some areas of Canada it was thought right to have Senators in addition to members of the House of Commons. In terms of population alone, neither of the territories really deserves representation in this House. In other words, there is an over-weighting even on the basis of their representation by one member each. After all, my own constituency has four times the population of either of the territories, yet there is still equal membership.
I have no objection to that. Even without direct contact with the area it is easily recognizable that both hon. members who represent those areas today have a great physical problem in getting around to see all their constituents. Not only is it a physical problem, it is also monetary. Surely representation in this place on behalf of that vast territory, the Northwest Territories, and the geographically less extensive Yukon territory, would be enhanced by representation in the other place, and I cannot see why not.
I must say I find it rather difficult even to take half seriously the criticisms of the hon. member for Northwest Territories to the effect that there would be difficulty in finding people from the territories, that so many people would be disenfranchised and would not be entitled to appear in the Senate. I cannot agree with him there.

Yes. Let me say that if you really want to dig into it there are a lot of people, true northerners and not transplanted southerners, who are, without my trying to be in any way patronizing, wise and educated, and what we call natives of the Northwest Territories, and they would be an addition to the other place, as they are to this place. I would be the first to defend the appointment of my old friend Jim Gladstone to the Senate, at a time when a lot of people derided it. They said we were taking a prairie Indian and putting him in the Senate, and that, aw shucks, this would accomplish nothing.
However, the appointment of Senator Gladstone and the work he did among the native Indians to bring them to the position of voting, and then convincing them that they should exercise their right to vote, is an historical fact. Doubtless members recall the difference between the election of 1962-63 and other elections as to the exercise of the ballot. I was with Senator Gladstone, and I know that immediately following passage of the act in 1962 that allowed treaty Indians who hitherto had not had the right to vote to exercise their ballot, there was a great deal of suspicion and uneasiness. After all, this was something unknown. That this suspicion was dispelled was due largely to the efforts of Jim Gladstone.
I am sure there are scores and scores of people in the Northwest Territories and Yukon, whether they be Indian, Eskimo or, not strangers to the place, but white men who were born and raised there, and who have the spirit of the Northwest Territories in their blood just as much as anybody else in the provinces have the spirit of the provinces in their blood, who would be suitable for appointment.
This might offer the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) an opportunity to change his policy with regard to appointments to the Senate. He could take some independent-minded people and those of other parties and appoint them to the Senate, considering the value of the individual concerned for his or her own intrinsic worth and the contribution that they could make.

Madam Speaker, though the government justifies this bill saying that the Northwest Territories and the Yukon will be better represented, I feel that it is ill-advised, and find it difficult to accept the increase in size of a group that is neither elected nor, in fact, representative of the population.

Mr. Speaker, I find it very difficult to accept this bill and I intend to vote against it. I do not oppose it because I quarrel with the legitimate desire of northerners to have additional voices here in Ottawa, and that is certainly one of the aspects which is on the plus side for northerners. My objection is that while we are talking about Senate reform we should not be proceeding in the direction of increasing the size of that place, at least before we have given serious consideration to such proposed reform. I think the government is out of line completely in moving on this bill now. It has made promises over the last generation, and certainly in the last few years I have been here-

-the government has made promises to move toward Senate reform, yet we are here debating a measure to increase the size of that body which is nonrepresentative and non-elected. We should not be doing this. We are going to increase the size of the representation of the Northwest Territories in this House when the next election occurs. We have passed that bill, and it seems to me that the change we are discussing today could have waited until we had an indication of the direction we intend to take on Senate reform. In spite of the fact that northerners may feel they are getting some kind of additional representation by having two senators, the method that has been generally used in selecting senators up to now does not lend much support to the theory that they are really representing anyone.

I would argue that northerners need more visits from members of the House of Commons. We have a committee that is responsible for Indian affairs and northern development. That committee put itself on record as being in favour of annual visits to each of the territories. It is part of the function of that committee, perhaps not all of its members at one time but the members of sub-committees appointed for that purpose, to visit the north on a regular basis, listening to the people and supplying them with an additional means of influencing the decisions made here in Ottawa.
The people in the north are in a different constitutional category from other Canadians in that these areas are not provinces. Judging by size of population, it will be a long time before they become provinces. Major changes have taken place in the viewpoint of Canadians toward resources generally. We now realize that there is perhaps no more important element in our economy than the natural resources spread across the country, 40 per cent of which are located within these two territories if our geological theorists are to be believed. Those two territories represent approximately 40 per cent of the total land mass of this country.
Given this change in the Canadian attitude toward resources, I think it is reasonable to expect changes in our thinking on the constitutional development of these Territories in the coming years. This bill is a mindless sort of move to implement promises of the past. It is an unthinking-forward motion resulting from past promises and it is ill-timed. Because of the prior need for Senate reform and possible changes in our thinking and approach to the constitutional evolution of the Northwest and Yukon Territories, I intend to vote against the bill.

Madam Speaker, I should like to make one or two comments prior to the passage of this motion on Bill C-3. After listening to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), I got the impression that while he is consistent in his view about rejecting acceptance of the Senate out of hand, he feels that if a person agrees with his point of view he must be serious, but if he does not he must somehow be looking at this matter in a flippant way. While I appreciate the hon. member's consistency in his point of view, I find it a little difficult to accept that idea. I do not accept that kind of condemnation.
In respect of representation of the north and Senate reform generally, I appreciate the views expressed by the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson). As parliamentarians, we are liable to a lot of criticism as a result of the impression held by many Canadians about the role of the Senate. According to the terms of the British North America Act, the Senate has two very specific functions to perform. It is supposed to be the place of sober second thought on legislation passed by this House. When you consider the age of some of us, perhaps that sober second thought is needed more today than ever before. That is a matter of opinion.
In the past, the Senate has performed many useful services to the parliamentary process. It has taken a second look at legislation and has possibly seen it from another perspective. From that point of view, the existence of the Senate is of real value. This takes me directly
Senate Representation
to the subject of area representation. It is said that the Senate is based on area representation but I do not believe for one minute that anyone in this House would really try to support that argument. Senate representation is really approached or accepted on the basis of compromise. If area representation in the Senate is to be valid, a new formula of representation will have to be considered during our discussions on Senate reform.
When we have a situation where a province such as Quebec or Ontario has 24 senators while the whole of the west has 24, I do not believe we have area representation. Also, I believe senators have been appointed through the political process. Often they have received their appointments for political favours given in the past. This process has been followed by both Liberals and Conservatives. In this way senators are compromised: when they reach the Senate they will not bite the hand that feeds them.
We have heard the arguments in respect of provincial rights with relation to natural resources. In that case, do we hear the members of the other place fulfilling their role as area representatives or, rather, do we hear them voicing the official party position on this question? It is my thinking with regard to a review of the British North America Act that it is incumbent upon senators to find out what the area views are and to express them no matter to what political party they belong. If there is to be Senate reform, senators first and foremost should protect provincial or area rights rather than vote according to official party lines.
In the joint committee on the constitution a recommendation was made that representation from the west be increased by 12 senators. I do not believe that in any way addresses itself to the problem. I do not believe that by this means area representation would be improved. While I support Bill C-3 in principle because I want to see representation from the north, I do not believe for a minute it contributes to the principle to which I am referring. It is my opinion that if the Senate is to be representative of the areas of Canada, it should reflect that representation on the basis of numerical equality rather than on the misconstrued formula which we have at the present time.
One of the objections that we as public officials receive comes from people who in effect ask what the senators are doing. They ask whether they are simply being paid off for favours rendered in the past and whether they simply become the right arm of the political machine or organization of the party to which they belong. I raise this matter very sincerely, Madam Speaker. I do not believe it is in the interest of parliament or the attitude we want to develop within the Canadian public, namely, of respect for the parliamentary process, that senators should take on a leading role in the party to which they belong.
The image of the Senate and parliament which the public seems to receive is that an attempt is being made to perpetuate the political process of the various parties rather than to carry out the responsibilities under the BNA Act, which are, primarily, that the Senate be a sober second-thought legislative body and that there be area representation. I say seriously that I do not see area

representation being given a very prominent position. I suggest that when members of the Senate take leading roles within the party, it compromises their position as senators in respect of their first responsibility and also destroys the confidence of the Canadian public in respect of the parliamentary process.
Senators are paid from the funds of the taxpayers. If they spend the majority of their effort in the interests of their parties, surely this is not the role of senators. I should like to see reform in that regard. This might not necessarily be related to Senate reform, but I think it is incumbent on all parties today to see that the Senate performs its constitutional role rather than a role which might be politically expedient at a given time.
In respect of reform of the Senate other than the question of area representation to which I have referred, the political question and the salaries senators receive, I believe senators should be appointed for a certain period of time. I do not believe the qualification in respect of age 75 is really any great factor. I think senators should be appointed, for example, for a five-year period and that the Prime Minister should have the constitutional right to reappoint them for one further term, let us say, for a total period of ten years.
In that way I feel a senator would know he had a specific period in which to work in the Senate, and because of that might fulfil his responsibility more faithfully. If a senator had fulfilled his responsibility, he would be eligible for a second term. I think this is a concept which should be examined. The public image of the Senate might be enhanced, because the people would know that senators were appointed for a period in order to provide service to their country.
I am in favour of the Senate. I want to see these reforms take place in order that the Senate may function better. I reject out-of-hand suggestions concerning abolition of the Senate. I want to see the bicameral system continue. Having said that, however, I believe that when there are difficulties we must not hide our heads in the sand and say there is no cure. I believe that when it becomes apparent that changes will take place, a change in public opinion will be reflected. So I intend to support this bill but, again, I wish to stress that we should seriously look at Senate reform and not merely talk about it. We should bear in mind that the Fathers of Confederation saw the Senate as a necessary function of the political process.

To a certain degree, in the recent debate on this question the point has been missed. We are not talking about whether or not the Senate of Canada should continue to exist. It does exist. The bill before us is not a bill to do away with the Senate; it is simply a bill to make it a more representative national institution. That is what we are discussing, not the future usefulness or function of the Senate. The precise question is whether the two great northern territories which occupy so much of our land mass and affect so much of the future of this country should be represented in an institution which calls itself national. I think the answer to that question is clear, and that it should be so representative.
It is clear to many of us who have had anything to do with northern policy that the people of the territories have too often been incidental victims of other ideas, other ideologies and other policies proposed for other purposes here. I believe that they are the incidental victims of the policy of colonialism which, unfortunately, is rampant in
April 18, 1975

the northern development section of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development because there is a determination among several well entrenched bureaucrats there to hold on to power in the northern territories. The capacity of the people of those two territories to have some degree of self-government has been delayed for far too long.
I,	for one, would most strenuously oppose any suggestion that they should be made victims of a simple dislike of the other place by some members of the House. I think they have suffered too much from being the victims of particular ideologies that happen to seize either individual members of the House or individual public servants. I think that if the Senate is to be a national body, it must represent those people and allow them this extra opportunity to have their views expressed and their opinions count here in the whole parliament of Canada.
Let me deal for a moment with the problems of the Senate-and no one would sweep them under the rug. Of course there has been patronage, and of course it has been perpetrated by prime ministers from this party-on the rare occasions we have had them-and prime ministers from the other party. Of course, as the anecdote I recounted earlier about the late, distinguished premier of Saskatchewan indicated, the same motive would have been followed by an NDP government, given the chance. But the fact that patronage has existed does not mean, and has not meant, that some effectiveness of the Senate has been totally undermined. Quite the opposite: there have been some very effective initiatives taken and effective roles played by the Senate despite the patronage.
My colleague, the hon. member for Northwest Territories, I understand raised a good point, that the present appointment requirements involving property and a certain amount of money may well militate against the appointment of native citizens in the two territories. That is a very serious fault and I hope it will be possible at least to consider some means to ensure that the native people, who in the Northwest Territories compromise the majority of the population, will have an equal opportunity to be named to the two new appointments if this House and the whole parliament agrees to create them.
I share the reservations expressed by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), and by others in this debate and elsewhere, about some of the recent practices of the Liberal Party in turning the Senate, in effect, into a political organization room for the Liberal Party and installing their chief executives, their chief fund raisers and chief propagandists in the other place so they can do their partisan work at public expense. That is a practice which, clearly, should be stopped. But the fact that that shameful practice is carried on as one of the functions of the Senate should not obscure our vision of the importance of the Senate on other fronts.
In my view-and I do not often offer congratulations to my colleagues across the way-there has been some modest progress in the appointments to the other place in the last number of years and, indeed, not simply in the last number of years. My own province is represented by at least two senators who clearly got there by merit, namely, Senator Donald Cameron from my own constituency, the founder of the Banff School of Fine Arts, and Senator
Senate Representation
Ernest Manning who served with distinction and success for so long as the premier of my province. Neither of them can be called Pavlovian Liberals who support the government every time it twitches. Indeed, I think that the recent evidence of independence in the Senate indicates that there has been a greater inclination on the part of the Liberals appointed there to question what the treasury benches do than we have found among the backbenchers of the Liberal Party in this House. There has been a much greater inclination for them to stand up for what they believe than there has been among some of my backbench colleagues on the other side.
Having regard to the recent record of my colleague, the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson), who spoke before me and who has left, I think that perhaps the consistent independence he has shown in this debate and others will stand him in good stead and at least offers one qualification for his elevation to the other place. Certainly, his independence would make him more at home there than it does here in the back benches of the Liberal Party.
I want to deal for moment with the suggestion that we have some sort of pure democratic system here to which the Senate is a singular affront. We have no such pure system. We have never had a system of direct democracy where one man equalled one vote. My own constituency is an example of the problems of that principle in a country as large as Canada. I represent an area of 40,000 square miles and a population smaller than that of many of my colleagues, such as the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski) and others who represent more compact urban areas. We have always recognized that it is in the nature of this country to allow for some variation in the principle of pure democracy. The Senate is not the single exception to that rule; there have been several others. It is, to say the least, unfair to try to single out the Senate for attack as being undemocratic in one sense or another.
The importance of the Senate-my colleague the hon. member for Provencher and others have made this point- is that it retains the capacity in the Parliament of Canada to ensure some kind of representation for the regions of Canada. That has always been important in a country that is as diverse and as liable to splinter apart as is this country, because it ensures that whatever might happen in an election there will be a vehicle open to the government to draw upon a region where it might not have been successful politically, for advice, for counsel and for the participation in government of outstanding men and women from that particular region or province.

The rationale of our Senate, in part, is that we must never overlook the importance to Canada of keeping in touch with the diversity and regional variation in this country. Of course, it has sometimes fallen down in that role, but the capacity is there. I suggest this is a capacity which is particularly important now because of the secret changes that have been introduced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in his attempt to centralize authority in a small group reporting to him and his office. This is a group which more and more reflects his own particular prejudice, even as all our views are particular and prejudiced. It reflects his own prejudiced view of the country.

By appointing people who share his particular perspective of Canada, whether it is the president of the CBC, the Clerk of the Privy Council, or whatever, he has moved away from the traditional idea that the people who make the decisions in this country should reflect as much as possible the diversity of the country. Instead of choosing those people, he has tried to choose people in his own image, and that only reflects a part of the country. At a time like this, when a system of government is being smuggled in which increasingly centralizes power in the image of the Prime Minister, it is doubly important that we maintain and strengthen an institution which can speak for the regions of Canada.
This is precisely what the bill would allow us to do in a small way. It would ensure that regions such as the north, which perhaps more than any other is left out of the day to day considerations of the centralized group who run things, would at least have the right of representation in the second chamber of the Parliament of Canada. I think that is an important innovation and one which we in this House should applaud.
I want to deal now with the opportunity that members from southern Canada have to become acquainted with the special problems of that unique region, the north. It is a region which is unique not only in Canada but in the world. It is a region which is little known to most of us here, although some of us have had an opportunity to visit it. The hon. member for Laprairie-the next senator from the Liberal side-had the opportunity to visit the north, as he told us, as a member of the standing committee.
It is clear that the composition of the population, the nature of development, the delicacy of the ecology, the capacity for exploitation of mineral development and the consequences of that exploitation, are different from the problems in other parts of Canada. It is, therefore, important that there be some continuing way in which both chambers of the Parliament of Canada, which are responsible as a whole for deciding the destiny of this country, should reflect that particular and peculiar part of the country. Of course, it is important, as the hon. member for Laprairie indicated, that the standing committee and other members of parliament should visit that unique region as often as possible.
It is helpful that the publicity attending the Berger inquiry and other such inquiries has increased an awareness in southern Canada of what is going on in the north. Some things have increased our understanding of that region, but certainly the government has been deficient in allowing a greater degree of self-government for those areas and not ending the colonial rule of the region. It is too mature and important to be ruled by a bunch of bureaucrats in an ivory tower in Ottawa.
The government has acted too often to limit the capacity of the north to make its own decisions. This bill is an exception to that general practice and allows an opportunity for the people of the territories and the interests and peculiar nature of the territories to be better known in the whole parliament of Canada. While I agree that this could be achieved in other ways, that fact should not negate the necessity and wisdom of pursuing this particular path. That is all we are being asked to do here. We are not being asked to pass judgment on the Senate of Canada, on

whether there should be a Senate. We are not even being asked to pass judgment on the practice of institutionalizing the Liberal Party and its political arm in the Senate. We are simply being asked to make that institution, which like this one is supposed to be a national institution, one which is national in fact. I think this is an important initiative and it is one which I intend to support. I regret having to commend the President of the Privy Council for anything, but I commend him for bringing forward this measure and I intend to support it.

The appointments that have been made, and the role taken by the Senate in the six or seven years that I have been here, have given me a new appreciation of the part that the Senate can play. Whether the appointments are political or, as the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark) has said, are made on the basis of individual talent and ability, I think there is a role for the Senate to play. I do not think anyone would detract from the excellence of the report on the media that was made by that staunch and persuasive Liberal, Senator Keith Davey. There was also Senator Croll's report on poverty which I commend to all hon. members for reading or rereading.
The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) said that senators would do nothing to bite the hand that feeds them. ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: LAKE WINNIPEG, MAN.-SUGGESTED FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL PROGRAM TO PREVENT FURTHER EROSION OF SHORELINE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should take action to initiate a program in conjunction with the government of Manitoba to prevent further erosion of Lake Winnipeg shoreline through the construction of adequate breakwaters, pilings and rip rap.
He said: Madam Speaker, with reference to Manitoba in general, and Lake Winnipeg in particular, as far as can be determined the three levels of government, particularly the federal and provincial governments, have engaged in little or no concentrated action to lessen the effects of erosion. There was a study announced by the then environment minister, Jack Davis, on September 29, 1971, costing $2 million and to be completed by the end of 1974. Its purpose was:
-to determine the effects that regulation of Lake Winnipeg, diversion of water from the Churchill River and development of the hydroelectric power potential of the Churchill River diversion route are likely to have on water and related resource uses.
Environmental Affairs
It was also to recommend ways of increasing over-all benefits from these projects. The Canada-Manitoba agreement noted that both governments are anxious to ensure that planned water resource developments achieve the greatest possible benefits without unduly prejudicing the present or potential development of these water bodies for other uses. These include water supply, fisheries, wildlife, recreation and transportation.
The Manitoba government initiated studies of erosion and sand movement along the shoreline of Lake Winnipeg. These will be incorporated into the studies authorized under the agreement. Broad guidelines were provided for the studies, involving investigations into the effects of the power development of the water regime, including water levels and flows, erosion, sedimentation and water supply. They will also cover effects on the uses of water and related resources, including community supply, fisheries, wildlife, recreation and tourism, navigation, forestry, land use, mining and historic sites. Social implications were also to be investigated by the board, which I expect will propose means of avoiding undesirable effects on people in the area and suggest how they can gain the greatest social and economic advantage from the development and activities arising out of it.
I commend the governments involved for their efforts. However, the report has not been made public to date and the people of Manitoba are as much in the dark as ever. I understand that the Canadian Centre for Inland Water has proposed a study of Lake Winnipeg which would include environmental aspects, particularly soil erosion. The government of Manitoba has given no indication to the federal government whether or not it intends to proceed at this stage with a joint study. We are awaiting an answer from Manitoba.
I would say this: simply identifying the problem is not enough. At the present time we are awaiting a report on the situation on the Nelson and Churchill rivers. Simply to understand what is taking place in relation to shoreline erosion is not good enough. It is incumbent upon federal and provincial governments that some kind of protective action be considered. I am certain that such measures will be found necessary. What should be the twofold purpose of these studies? The first should be to identify the problem, and the second should take whatever measures are necessary in terms of the prevention of erosion.
I expect the response of the government to this motion will be to the effect that the subject does not specifically fall within federal jurisdiction. Madam Speaker, I wish to bring to your attention examples of federal participation in the conservation of shoreline properties. I cite in particular what has been done in connection with the St. Lawrence, the St. Clair and the Detroit rivers. The federal government sought to ascertain the amount of damage resulting from what I might call unnatural causes, specifically, in these cases, the movement of ships up and down the rivers. The river bank was zoned in accordance with the percentage of damage by erosion attributed to waves caused by the movement of ships. The property owner concerned would then get an estimate of the cost of preventing erosion. He submitted this estimate to the Department of Public Works and in turn the department would

Environmental Affairs
authorize the payment of that percentage of the cost of protection payable under the formula-the percentage of erosion caused by, shall I say, the human factor, in this case shipping. I put it to the minister that the erosion of the shoreline of Lake Winnipeg is also due to human causes, and I suggest that the federal government should participate in the cost of remedial measures to the same degree as it has in the case of the three rivers I have mentioned.
In the last few years in Manitoba, Manitoba Hydro has embarked upon a number of extensive development projects. One of these is known as Genpeg. It is no secret in Manitoba and elsewhere that the potentialities of Genpeg can only be realized if Lake Winnipeg can be used as a reservoir. The corporation intends to raise the average level of the lake from 713 feet to 715 feet by a system of locks, and so on, thereby assuring a reservoir which would provide a constant current for the project. Because of the unnaturally high levels which are constantly maintained, excessive erosion is now a fact. As we saw earlier, where there is a factor in erosion other than natural conditions, the federal government has chosen to take an active interest. Today we see, on Lake Winnipeg, similar conditions, conditions not caused by natural phenomena but by human intervention, by human construction. Erosion of the shoreline has been caused by those factors. I submit that excessive shoreline erosion is taking place as a result of human interference in raising the level of the lake from 713 feet to 715 feet. I do not propose that the federal government should accept full responsibility for the prevention of this erosion of the shoreline. Nevertheless, I believe it would be equitable if the federal government were to participate on the basis of the same formula as applied to the cases I have mentioned.
It would be remiss of me if I were not to say that there is, in fact, the possibility of preventing shoreline erosion. In case the minister may wish to allocate the necessary funds immediately, I propose to outline a scheme upon which the minister can spend this money, if he wishes to do so, starting at the beginning of next week. A number of schemes have been aired by leading engineers in Manitoba, and the one which particularly strikes my fancy, since it is within the easiest economic reach of the federal government, involves a system of groins to be constructed along the shoreline of the lake. Take the stretch of the lake where erosion is most prevalent-around the Sandy Hook area; take a stretch of five miles and build groins, 62 of them, 100 feet in length, running 30 degrees with the coast and extending one mile into the lake, and set them 500 or 600 feet apart. The phenomenon caused by a system of groins is well known. As a result of the currents created by these groins existing along the shoreline, back of the groins there is a field of sand, so that you get natural beaches and the only erosion that takes place is just before the groins at the far end. So that over this stretch of five miles along which these groins are actually constructed there would be virtually no shoreline erosion.
I was quite prepared to do some homework for the minister so that he would not have to run around getting figures for himself, and I inquired in terms of cubic yards of material what the cost would be, whether the material

was really available, and so on. I do not want to suggest a solution if in fact we have to lug the rocks from Nova Scotia. Consider the fact that this five-mile stretch attracts thousands of Manitobans. It would take only
50,000	yards of material to cover this stretch, and this could be acquired as at the end of this month. If the government does not get inflation under control in the month of May, the costs might be somewhat higher; but assuming that the cost remains the same for May, it would be $10.95 a yard delivered and in place.
If you multiply this figure by the 50,000 yards required, it will cost $549,500. Then there is roughly $90,000 additional labour cost. So for total protection forever and ever, or at least for the next 100 years or so, for some $639,500 we can beat shoreline erosion on this stretch of shoreline of which I am speaking of some five miles. We are not talking about billions of dollars of expenditure; we are talking probably of only 40 to 50 miles at the maximum along which this system of groins and rip-rapping, piledriving and possibly breakwaters would have to be constructed. When I make an estimate, Madam Speaker, I like to be accurate and conservative. Perhaps the minister is not familiar with the process of accuracy in estimates, but the total amount required for the protection of the shoreline for all of Lake Winnipeg, with which we are vitally concerned, is within $1 million of $20 million.
I am watching the clock and I notice that my time is almost up, so in summary let me say this: I do not believe that the federal government is justified in continuing an attitude toward shoreline erosion that is indistinguishable from that exemplified by the flat earth society. Shoreline erosion on Lake Winnipeg is, and will continue to be, caused in great part by the human element.
I want to stress again that in the cases I have cited where the human element has caused erosion, the federal government has been willing to participate. I am calling for a very similar and equitable attitude on the part of this government with reference to Lake Winnipeg in particular, and generally for all those areas of western Canada where shoreline erosion is attributed to these factors. Using a similar formula, the federal government is now obliged, because of the sheer magnitude of the issue and the reasonableness of my arguments, to make funds available immediately for this project.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Turner (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: LAKE WINNIPEG, MAN.-SUGGESTED FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL PROGRAM TO PREVENT FURTHER EROSION OF SHORELINE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to commend the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway) for bringing this problem to the attention of the government. I should like to speak on behalf of the Department of Public Works. The Department of Public Works is not responsible for shoreline erosion due to natural causes. It does, however, accept responsibility for shoreline damage or erosion which has been caused by wave action from commercial shipping or through the presence of a federal structure such as a breakwater, wharf or other harbour works. Where erosion is caused by natural forces and remedial measures are considered necessary, it is the responsibility of the riparian owner to initiate a remedial program. Where erosion arises from high water levels and flooding and a disaster situation exists, a number of federal government agencies could provide assistance to the
April 18, 1975

province concerned consistent with pertinent federal policy.
I should like to bring that policy to the attention of the House. The British North America Act delegates responsibility for the control of navigation to the federal government. A cabinet directive on remedial works recorded on November 6, 1966, provided for federal government participation in remedial works where erosion is caused by commercial navigation or the presence of a federal government structure. On behalf of the government, the Department of Public Works has been discharging the responsibility of constructing protective works along shores of the St. Lawrence River and other navigable waters where waves from commercial navigation cause erosion. The department also considers erosion to be its responsibility when a government structure is deemed the cause of erosion and when a government property is threatened by erosion from natural causes such as waves, currents, seepage, rain, frost, ice, etc.
It is realized that there should be some reasonable relationship between the cost of the protection work to be built and the value of the property to be protected, otherwise the government could be blamed for having built costly works for the protection of properties of very little value. To ensure that a fair and reasonable relationship criteria is applied, the 1966 cabinet directive was amended and approved by cabinet on May 2, 1974. All memoranda on this subject written prior to the introduction of the revised policy, excluding reference to criteria and guidelines developed by the Department of Public Works, are superseded.
The revised policy is summarized as follows. The Department of Public Works is authorized to construct remedial works and assume the total cost of such works in the event that more than 50 per cent of the erosion can be attributed to navigation or a federal government structure and the value of the land or property to be protected is equal to, or greater than, the cost of such remedial works. Where erosion results mainly from natural causes but where navigation or the presence of a federal government structure is a contributing factor, the Department of Public Works may contribute to the cost of such remedial works in proportion to the effect these causes have on erosion. Contributions will be based on a cost that DPW considers sufficient to provide adequate protection. The Department of Public Works continue to carry out minimum maintenance of such works in accordance with the terms of the policy.
Headquarters and regions will ensure that all remedial works are evaluated in accordance with the terms of the amended policy, and where investigations indicate federal government responsibility, that the degree of government contribution is clearly established through the application of supporting criteria developed by the department. Where supporting criteria is considered inadequate in complex cases clearly to define the degree of government responsibility, it will be the responsibility of regions to identify the need for special studies or measurements and to report their recommendations to headquarters.
Erosion of the shorelines of lakes and rivers is a continuing natural process. The boundary between land and water is subject to constant changes and shifts due to
Environmental Affairs
natural causes, and occasionally man's activities. Erosion and its resulting problems for shoreline property owners occur throughout Canada. Unfortunately, historical development of shorelines has proceeded without a proper awareness of the process of erosion or of the constantly changing nature of the shorelines. All too often this has resulted in serious problems.
The rate of erosion depends on composition of the shoreline and the exposure of the shore to the natural weathering agents, especially currents and waves. In some cases, surface water run-off, ground water seepage, frost and ice action also contribute to erosion. Human activities sometimes intensify these natural erosion processes and cause additional damage. From the environmental point of view it is often a wise rule not to interfere with nature's shoreline processes. The eroded materials usually contribute to building of beaches in other locations and the formation and maintenance of offshore sand bars and islands. However, erosion of shorelines has often led to financial hardship and personal losses. In some cases government action is necessary, but in the case of Lake Winnipeg the federal government is limited in its choice of action.
In most cases erosion affects private property directly. Under the British North America Act, matters concerning property rights normally fall under provincial and municipal jurisdiction. Thus, the federal government has not usually contributed to the construction of erosion protection works. The federal government does have responsibilities related to navigation, fisheries, and in connection with the management of international and interprovincial waters. In special cases, then, it assumes, through the Department of Public Works, some responsibility for protecting shores from erosion caused by commercial navigation or due to the presence of federal structures. Under these circumstances, the federal government has spent about $30 million on the construction and maintenance of shore protective works since 1947.
Where shore erosion can be traced to waves generated by commercial navigation, the Department of Public Works will construct dikes and bank stabilization works to protect the shoreline. If more than 50 per cent of the erosion at a location is caused by marine transport, and if the land to be protected is worth at least twice the cost of remedial works, the Department of Public Works will assume all project costs. If transport or federal structures contribute to less than one-half of the erosion at a site, the department may assume up to 50 per cent of project costs.
In the case of Lake Winnipeg, the government does not consider that the appropriate conditions exist for federal participation in erosion protection projects. Neither commercial navigation nor federal structures contribute in any significant way to the natural erosion forces. Windgenerated waves on this large, open body of water are the main causes of weathering of the shoreline. Furthermore, Lake Winnipeg is neither an international nor an interprovincial body of water and the jurisdiction over property rights lies with provincial authorities.
If, in the judgment of provincial authorities, the erosion problem is serious enough to be considered of national

April 18, 1975
Environmental Affairs
concern, the federal government is willing to discuss the situation. Appropriate mechanisms have been established under the Canada Water Act for joint federal-provincial studies and action in matters of significant national interest. However, in general the federal government is very reluctant to impinge on the provinces' prerogatives in this matter. There is, therefore, no readily apparent justification for federal involvement either directly or in co-operation with the provincial government. Indeed, to federally fund protection bank stabilization works in this instance might create a precedent that could have multibillion dollar ramifications throughout the country.
Nineteenth century thinking demanded that man conquer and tame nature, but human existence is not necessarily a battle against nature. Today we are realizing that perhaps the best course of action is to live in harmony with our environment and the forces of nature. It has been said that flood damages are not cuased by an act of God but by acts of men. The same can be said of erosion damages. It is this government's view that in many cases the most desirable solution to the problem is not the provision of structural works but the introduction of land management practices designed to discourage development on erosion prone shorelines.
