speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I should like to take part in this debate for a few minutes, not so much because I have an in-depth knowledge of these problems on Lake Winnipeg but, rather, because I have some general concern along the same line in relation to Lake Ontario, particularly the Scarborough bluffs, and perhaps because I have some background in working in this area as a result of professional training.
We should take a look at the matter of erosion control as introduced by the motion of the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway). The previous speaker pretty well outlined the official position of the Department of Public Works and the federal responsibility. Federal responsibility is in the area of navigable waters and damage relating directly to the use of such waters, taking into account the cost of the work in relation to the amount of damage.
I was rather impressed by the approach of the Canadian government to erosion problems. The hon. member for Selkirk raised a question about the time-frame involved and I think his concern is justified. In terms of the government's approach to this problem, I am not sure how widely distributed is the report resulting from the study of shoreline erosion on the St. Lawrence River and Great Lakes system. This is a good document in terms of its inventory of those areas that have been damaged, or could be damaged, and the extent. This is much like carrying out a school board inventory of the school repairs necessary and deciding which school needs the repairs most. I do not think you can go ahead with projects in many of these areas until you have made an inventory of the existing problems. The consultative process that flows from this very necessarily involves the provinces.
I hope the report resulting from the study in Manitoba of erosion damage on Lake Winnipeg will soon be forthcoming. I differ with the hon. member in that I believe it will be up to the province of Manitoba to invite federal participation and assistance in this area. I understand the causes of erosion in the area are two, namely, falling water

levels and substantial wave action due to unprecedented winds.
One of the results of hydroelectric power projects is the alteration to a substantial degree of water levels. This is something the governments involved, whether federal or provincial, will have to take into account in dealing with these changing levels. Whenever there is a change in the water level, nature takes its course and re-establishes the shoreline. Those shorelines along our lakes and rivers which are not subject to erosion are shorelines that have experienced a fair amount of erosion in days past, with the soil and material that can be eroded having gone, leaving a granular base that is pretty well erosion free.
I have looked at a number of hydroelectric projects in which I have been interested over the years and have found that much of the damage to the environment has resulted in nature re-establishing shorelines that are essentially erosion-proof. I think it is absolutely necessary, in terms of hydroelectric projects, that this type of analysis and assessment be done ahead of time. I think the remedy proposed by the hon. member for Selkirk is good, but it should have been established before any change in the water level so that nature might have worked to establish the new level.
I have some knowledge of the structure of municipalities, and so on, surrounding lakes and I assume that if Lake Winnipeg is like most lakes of this size it has several municipalities perhaps of differing financial straits and ability to deal with such a program. I was associated with the conservation authority in Ontario some years ago. I was very impressed with the role played by that authority. At one time it was really responsible for the watershed policies in respect of navigation and drainage of the lakes and larger rivers into the conservation and water conserving projects there.
It is of interest, perhaps, to the hon. member that at the present time, in the city of Toronto, all of the shoreline associated with the greater metropolitan area has been turned over to the metropolitan and district conservation authorities in terms of the water shoreline development as well as erosion and shoreline maintenance. This has been done because the province of Ontario has taken the view that perhaps of all the bodies which might be involved in this, this group of people with the overview it has, not only in respect of the shoreline but because of having jurisdiction over the entire watershed, is perhaps the best qualified body to deal with the shoreline itself.
In terms of some of the remedial action the hon. member is suggesting, I think the establishment of a conservation authority, founded essentially by the province but contributed to by each of the municipalities through which the watershed flows, and in some instances by the federal government, is a very good approach to take. I believe it was back in 1954 that we had hurricane Hazel. At that time my riding and particularly the adjacent riding were very drastically affected by the flash flood. There was tremendous erosion not only of the watershed area draining the Humber River system and the metropolitan area, but also on the lakefront, involving loss of life and property. That was really the impetus for the establishment of
April 18, 1975

the conservation authorities which have been able to turn much of the land subject to flooding and bad erosion more or less over to public ownership, on the basis that the land would be used for recreational purposes. With the tremendous growth that we have in urban areas, I think it is almost impossible to satisfy the need for recreational facilities. Much of the remedial work and programs of the authority have been compatible with using the land, when restored, for recreational purposes. I think really this is the only way to accomplish this.
I think quite often when we speak about erosion problems in respect of shorelines, we are specifically interested in a particular shoreline and how it might be repaired at a reasonable cost and in a proper engineering manner. I believe we quite often forget that a good deal of the problem may originate inland, and that we must take a very close look at the entire watershed in terms of agriculture, conservation practices and what the over-all land use practices are.
I have some knowledge of the Great Lakes. From year to year when water levels vary as they do, particularly when the level is high, there is a tremendous amount of erosion and much of that problem results from some very questionable municipal zoning which allows structures to be built in areas which, to the practical eye, are very prone to damage. I think zoning is another area of municipal responsibility in this regard.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is with some trepidation that I rise to join in this discussion this afternoon since I, like the previous speaker, have little knowledge of the actual physical conditions of which the hon. member opposite speaks when he describes the problems that caused him to present this motion. He made reference to the problems around Lake Winnipeg. My riding borders on Lake Erie, one of the Great Lakes which has experienced substantial difficulty from erosion. Considerable assistance has been granted by the federal government in the form of studies along the lakeshore to determine what are the sources of difficulty and what might be a potential cure for these problems.
Along Lake Erie and Lake St. Clair, and indeed-to bring it into context with what the hon. member has said-along the Detroit River and the St. Clair River there has been substantial damage caused by high water. Much damage is experienced from year to year as a result of wind conditions and shipping in this area. I suggest that the federal government, by its proposals and policies described by the parliamentary secretary, has recognized that in certain cases, in fact, the damage has been caused or has resulted from the construction of some type of federal work or work it has permitted to be done in the navigation area. In many cases the erosion has been caused by wave action.
There is no question that when in the area of $30 million was spent by the federal government on the St. Lawrence River system, Lake Erie, Lake St. Clair, the Detroit River and the St. Clair River, it was spent by reason of the fact that much of the destruction of land and property owned
Environmental Affairs
by private individuals was caused by the heavy wave action resulting from navigation. I have sat beside the river and seen what the wave action of a freighter can do: it is unbelievable.
I think the policy of the federal government, that there must be some reparation in respect of this type of damage, is sound. However, when I find in fact that there is no heavy shipping on Lake Winnipeg, I find it difficult to believe that the hon. member opposite can make the same point that is applicable to the St. Clair and the Detroit River system in respect of Lake Winnipeg and its shoreline. I was interested when the hon. member suggested that many engineering studies had taken place and that some of the conclusions of those studies seemed to be that the groins system might be the answer. He seemed to think this might be the answer for time immemorial, and then he cut down to perhaps 100 years.
I suggest to him that the same type of protection that he described has been tried with respect to Lake Erie. I would advise him that I would be happy at any time to take him into areas on the south border of my riding to show him what happens to the groins. The experience in the area of Lake Erie has been that a groin lasts perhaps 30 years, if you are lucky. They have tried all kinds of groins. They have tried them with timber and the gabion type, being wire mesh, stone filled. The latest method seems to be very large, armoured stone. The force of water is something to behold. It tears these great, man-made gabions out as if they were nothing.
I think of gabions that were put in in my riding less than 20 years ago. Now there is nothing left to bear witness to them except a few pieces of water-torn and ice-torn wood. It is true that there was a certain build-up of sand behind these gabions and then, for a certain period of time, they worked. But with the high water over the past two years, this sand is rapidly disappearing. I, along with the hon. member opposite, would like to be able to call on the federal government to give us some assistance in protecting the land that is rapidly being worn away. However, the fact that my constituents, as well as the constituents of the hon. member, are experiencing the same difficulties does not make it a federal problem. Surely we should look beyond this and consider the total cost as well as the precedent we would be setting in providing the kind of support which the hon. member seeks.
If there are difficulties such as I have described in my riding, and such as those described by the hon. member opposite along Lake Winnipeg, surely the same type of problems exist along all our coasts, inland or otherwise. If the federal government goes beyond the bounds described in its policies, it will enter into what is essentially provincial jurisdiction in protecting these shorelines, and I suggest that the cost would be too high for this fair land of ours to support. Even when expressed by the figure $20 million, which I think the hon. member opposite suggested for one project, if one multiplies that figure by the number of projects which would ultimately come before the federal government, one would be faced with a gargantuan sum.

April 18, 1975
Environmental Affairs
I think that the policy described by the parliamentary secretary is reasonable. It affords the opportunity to the federal government to take its share of the burden and, indeed, to accept the blame if in fact it has been responsible or should have some responsibility. It recognizes that there are certain instances when it is not just nature that is tearing away at the shorelines and that perhaps we should give some assistance; but I think it also does service to the separation of power between the provincial and federal jurisdictions, recognizing that the province has some obligation to do something within its borders as well.
I think recognition of that shared responsibility is accepted by other jurisdictions, and I point specifically to the jurisdiction of Ontario which I know best. The province recognizes, through its special emergency assistance programs, its disaster and relief assistance programs and its shoreline property assistance program-the list is long and I have looked at these various problems because I have experienced this type of difficulty in my constituency-that it has a substantial responsibility.
I suggest to the hon. member opposite that surely the province of Manitoba, in this instance, must also recognize that it has a responsibility, if indeed not the total responsibility, for dealing with the problem which he described. I might have a certain sympathy for the problem of the hon. member opposite by reason of shared experience, but I would have some difficulty in requesting the federal jurisdiction to change its policy position. I think the policy is sound and I think the federal government recognize their responsibilities. They recognize that there are difficulties with respect to shared responsibility with the provinces and that those responsibilities should not be breached.
Before concluding I should like to point out that in addition to the problem in the areas I have described in my riding, and indeed in the Lake Winnipeg area where erosion is taking place, there is the problem of land use and subsoil erosion. In my area there are high bluffs around Lake Erie which have been dropping into the lake. Notwithstanding the fact that for a number of years this process has been going on as a result of natural erosion, this has increased. There is some suggestion in the independent studies that have been made that the cause of this type of fall may be subsoil water that has been created by putting up new subdivisions which have created tremendous subsoil water loads from septic systems which flow toward the lake trying to seek their natural levels, thus creating potential slides which cause great chunks of land to fall in.
I think this example points out the necessity for the investigative program and study that the federal government has undertaken in the Lake Winnipeg area. Taking all these things together, I cannot support the motion of the hon. member although I sympathize with his reasons for bringing it forward. I suggest that perhaps he should seek further assistance from his constituents and from the provincial jurisdiction. For the reasons I have given, I am forced to speak against the motion.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, like the hon. member for Kent-Essex (Mr. Daudlin), I am in sympathy with the position stated by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway), but I

have to part company with the hon. member for Kent-Essex with respect to his statement that he would oppose the motion. Indeed, I give it my support. Admittedly, this problem of erosion of the shores of Lake Winnipeg must be shared provincially and federally; no one denies that, least of all the hon. member for Selkirk. It is also my understanding that the government of Manitoba has sought financial assistance from the federal government, and I hope that despite the possibility that this motion may not pass this afternoon, continued consideration and study will be given to this matter.
I can confirm the seriousness of the problem. This erosion is taking place on the west shore of Lake Winnipeg in the constituency of the hon. member for Selkirk, in the area to which he referred from Sandy Hook to Gimli. It also takes place on the east shore of Lake Winnipeg in the constituency of the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), north and south of Victoria Beach.
My interest in this subject of course is not only because of the fact that, like these two hon. members, I am a Manitoban, but also because quite a few people from the city of Winnipeg, part of which I have the honour to represent, have summer homes and cottages on both sides of Lake Winnipeg. When the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Turner) started to make his speech, I thought for a moment that perhaps the battle had been won. As he outlined the new criteria on the basis of which the federal government will make money available, I thought my hon. friend from Selkirk was going to win, but there seem to be different forms of logic around the place. I regret that at the end the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works, speaking on behalf of the government, came down with the negative reply that he gave today.
There certainly are many causes for the situation so far as Lake Winnipeg is concerned. Part of the trouble is because of navigation, but no one of us would claim that is the only reason. Part of it is weather and winds. Last summer, in particular, unusual winds resulted in very severe erosion on both sides of the lake. Some people thought that the trouble might be because of the provincial government's hydro work in the north, but it was pretty clear to the persons who were there that it was when the wind was blowing a certain way that most of the erosion took place.
From what has been said on behalf of the federal government, it strikes me that it recognizes it has to consider causes that are natural and part of the whole development of the surface of the earth, but that it also has to consider man-made causes. On all counts, it seems to me there is a case for the federal government to be interested in and to share the responsiblility of dealing with the problem that faces people on both sides of Lake Winnipeg.
I should like to express once again my support for the resolution presented this afternoon by the hon. member for Selkirk.

subsubtopic: LAKE WINNIPEG, MAN.-SUGGESTED FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL PROGRAM TO PREVENT FURTHER EROSION OF SHORELINE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, though I have no direct
April 18, 1975

interest in the erosion around Lake Winnipeg other than that of sharing the concerns of those who live along its shores, and the concern so well expressed by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway), I want to assure that hon. member that I share fully the views he expressed in this House, this afternoon and previously, for, although I do not come from Manitoba, I do represent a riding that suffers extreme erosion damages from the sea.
If I am not mistaken, until 1954 the government had a policy whereby it granted a certain amount annually to remedy, at least in part, this situation which has become most alarming. But since Canada, unlike Africa, has many streams, damages by erosion are therefore very extensive. In 1954 the government, faced with the enormous claims and costs involved-I was told that they could then even exceed the federal budget-decided in its wisdom, if we can call it that, to set guidelines that were described, I think, by the parliamentary secretary, stating the federal government would recognize its responsibility in cases of erosion due to shipping or the presence of structures erected by the federal government.
Those are the same guidelines that have been dinned into our ears for many years, since 1954, and which were reiterated recently by the Minister of Public Works in reply to a question asked by a member of the Social Credit Party. I believe it was the hon. member for Bellechasse.
At Chaleur Bay, in some places, there are 25 or 30 miles between the two shores, that of New Brunswick and that of the province of Quebec. One easily realizes that when a ship goes up Chaleur Bay to reach the ports of Dalhousie or Carleton for example, what impact the wake can have on the bayshore.
This can happen on the St. Lawrence River, relatively narrow at Quebec City and maybe somewhat more a little upstream, but among our criteria was the presence of federal structures. For eight years at least I, for one, have been pleading in favour of the numerous constituents
Environmental Affairs
located between two wharves built by the Department of Public Works and who unfortunately were unable to have protection walls erected to protect their buildings, first the barn and then the house, from falling down into Chaleur Bay.
So my argument is based on the presence of federal structures in the area. There are two such structures: one west and the other east. But that is not enough. The property is valued, and then it is found that such and such a percentage shall be paid by the municipality, another percentage by the owner and the balance by the federal government.
This can no longer be tolerated. As suggested in the motion by the hon. member for Selkirk, the federal government should do something since this is an area of mixed jurisdiction. I would even say it is almost exclusively provincial jurisdiction. Even considering what the federal government did in the past, the province submits this is under federal jurisdiction.
My constituents ask whether the waters are federal. Nowhere have I read that the waters in Chaleur Bay or elsewhere were federal waters. The problem should be settled once and for all, because the province cannot afford it alone. The owner with repairs to be done cannot pay the cost, neither can the municipality. There should be agreements of necessity, as soon as possible, between various levels of government so that the situation may be corrected, which has become very urgent in some instances. If our areas are to be developed, they should first be saved and protected.
